questions.knowledge_point: Identifying Integrals That Evaluate to Zero
questions.problem:
Which of the following integrals evaluates to zero due to symmetry?

- ${\int }_{-5}^{5}2{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-4}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-1}^{1}3{e}^{-x}\,\text{d}x$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to $0$ due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x)=2{x}^{4}$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =2(-x)^{4} \\  & =2{x}^{4} \\  & \ne -f(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

- The function $g(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(6(-x)) \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(-6x) \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x) \\  & =-g(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-4}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

- The function $f(x)=3{e}^{-x}$ is *not* an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =3{e}^{-(-x)} \\  & =3{e}^{x} \\  & \ne -f(x)\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.problem:
Which of the following integrals evaluates to zero due to symmetry?

- ${\int }_{-5}^{5}\frac{x}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x$
- ${\int }_{0}^{2}x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}x$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

So, to determine which integrals evaluate to $0$ due to symmetry, we have to determine which integrands are odd functions.

- The function $f(x)=\frac{x}{1+{x}^{2}}$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =\frac{(-x)}{1+(-x)^{2}} \\  & =-\frac{x}{1+{x}^{2}} \\  & =-f(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-5}^{5}\frac{x}{1+{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

- The function $g(x)={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is an odd function:

$$
\begin{aligned}g(-x) & =(-x)^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x) \\  & ={x}^{2}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =-{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =-g(x)\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by symmetry, we can conclude that

$$
{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

- The function $h(x)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+1)$ is an odd function, but integral III is not of the form ${\int }_{-a}^{a}h(x)\,\text{d}x$ since the upper and lower limits are not opposites. Therefore, we cannot use symmetry to simplify the integral.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.knowledge_point: Simplifying Definite Integrals of Odd Functions
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Notice that $f(x)={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is an odd function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =(-x)^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x) \\  & ={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(-x) \\  & ={x}^{2}(-\operatorname{sin}⁡x) \\  & =-{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)={x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ is an odd function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}{x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

questions.problem: Given that ${\int }_{0}^{10}2\sqrt[5]{x}\,\text{d}x=A,$ what is the value of ${\int }_{-10}^{0}2\sqrt[5]{x}\,\text{d}x?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the following:

- a function $f(x)$ is *even* if $f(-x)=f(x)$

- a function $f(x)$ is *odd* if $f(-x)=-f(x)$

Moreover, for any odd function $f(x),$ the graph of $y=f(x)$ has rotational symmetry of order $2$ about the origin, so we have

$$
{\int }_{-a}^{a}f(x)\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Notice that $f(x)=2\sqrt[5]{x}$ is an odd function. Indeed, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(-x) & =2\sqrt[5]{(-x)} \\  & =-2\sqrt[5]{x} \\  & =-f(x).\end{aligned}
$$

So, because $f(x)=2\sqrt[5]{x}$ is an odd function, we have

$$
{\int }_{-10}^{10}2\sqrt[5]{x}\,\text{d}x=0.
$$

Finally, using the adjacent intervals rule for integration, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-10}^{10}2\sqrt[5]{x}\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-10}^{0}2\sqrt[5]{x}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{10}2\sqrt[5]{x}\,\text{d}x & =0 \\ {\int }_{-10}^{0}2\sqrt[5]{x}\,\text{d}x+A & =0 \\ {\int }_{-10}^{0}2\sqrt[5]{x}\,\text{d}x & =-A.\end{aligned}
$$
